en: The Vajrasattva Pārājika. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!
Oṃ, homage to the Omniscient One!
Having paid homage to Vajrasattva, the protector of the world and the one of great compassion,
I shall describe the rules for expiation, as well as the conduct of purification and virtuous vows.
The teacher is the supreme deity and must be worshipped with great effort;
he is the King who holds the Vajra himself, abiding in manifest form. (2)
The killing of living beings and the expiation for it are described as the subject matter [of this section].
In that regard, [it concerns] those who observe the vows of a Vajrācārya and those belonging to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Because the executioner commits a great sin (mahāpātaka), the rules regarding them are now stated. ||3||
Furthermore, it is of two kinds, as follows:
And because it is called "self-made" (*svayaṃkṛta*) and so forth.
In that regard, that which is performed by means of one's own body or through the instigation of another person is called "self-performed" (svayaṃkṛta). ||4||
Even there, many become intent on speaking as soon as each one has arisen.
In that case, by what is it brought about that each [atom] becomes as one?
Because desire arises individually for each [object].
Therefore, that too is said to be self-made. ||5||
As it has been said:
Of many who perform a single task, all of whom are bearers of weapons.
If there is one killer therein, all of them are considered killers. ||6||

Furthermore, where he performs only the mere act of beating, threatening, and so forth, and does not, on account of that beating or other such cause, or with reference to that action, cause himself to be killed; [in that case, there is no offense]. ||7||
In that regard, the destruction of signs is to be understood.
And the sign (nimitta) has indeed been explained with effort in many ways, through its relations and so forth.
Whether reviled, beaten, or oppressed by the unfortunate, he who would give up his life on account of such a person is called a "protector" (pratighātaka). (19) 8.
But when one who has been seized by another seeks to see his evil deed and,
for that person's sake, gives up his life, they call him a "protector" (pratighātaka).

If one, afflicted by suffering, should give up their life for the sake of their own property or for the sake of someone in their own community, they call that person a "protector" (pratighātaka). ||10||
In the event of the seizure of cattle, land, gold, women, or the house of a Kṣatriya, he who gives up his life for that person is called a "protector" (pratighātaka). ||11||
Whether for the sake of purity, for the sake of one's father or mother, or even for the sake of meat.
They call him a "destroyer" (pratighātaka) with reference to whom one would give up one's life. ||12||
If any observer of a vow should give up his life through an unrelated cause, it is proclaimed by men that the sin belongs to that very person alone. (13)
Even if an assassin approaches with the intent to kill while one is well-prepared for battle, one may kill him with the desire to kill; by doing so, the practitioner does not violate his vow. //14//
Whether he be a teacher, a child, an elder, one observing a vow, or even one deeply learned, one should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation. (15)

(Compare: "Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin")—There is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in killing an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor), whether done openly or in secret; let there be no anger, for I ask you this. 16.
One may slay even an assassin born into a family of Vedic students; one who has been provoked by anger incurs no blame for that act.
The arsonist, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the abductor of land or wife—these six are known as *ātatāyin* (assassins). 18.

"No fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor), whether openly or in secret; rather, it is the wrath [of the victim] that overtakes him. However, if anyone should kill one who is observing a vow through ignorance...
But through consciousness, one should exert effort; the Noble One bestows grace.
(19) Now, regarding the occasion for the penance for killing those who observe vows, such as the Vajrācārya and others: (20)
The vow is now described, specifically for the purification of the sin arising from the killing of a Vajrācārya. ||1||
The rule for expiation shall apply for up to twelve years;
however, after eleven years, one is purified by the gift of wealth.
Jewels, pearls, gold, cattle, houses, gifts, and land.
Likewise, the excavation of lotus ponds and the like, as well as the erection of palaces and other structures. ||2||
Various ornaments and garments, as well as articles such as bell-metal and copper;
And even a man who has committed evil deeds should give those gifts with faith.
To a teacher who is proficient, to a monk endowed with virtuous conduct, and to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, [one should offer gifts] with devotion of body, speech, and mind. ||4||
To prevent a relapse and for the sake of non-liberation, one should offer all one's possessions.
Thus, for one who possesses wealth, there is the practice of giving; for one who is destitute, there is the recitation of mantras and so forth.
Indeed, he who observes the Poṣadha vow for even a single year should bathe daily at sacred fords (tīrthas) and perform circumambulation of the Caityas.
He should dwell constantly in the teacher’s house and disclose his faults in the monastery;
the hero, intent on reflecting upon the Dharma, should be self-controlled and conquer his senses.
For the sake of destroying great sins, one should practice celibacy;
one should also perform acts such as giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and worship, according to the prescribed rules for their commencement. ||8||
By means of expiation,
[and] subsequently by non-occurrence, as well as by following the proper sequence.
There may be eating at fixed times for one day, eating only at night for two days,
eating only what is unasked for three days, and fasting for four days.
If one desires [to perform it], it is said that one [recitation] should be performed every four days;
I shall prescribe the penance for that duration of three nights.
A practitioner of vows should perform the consecration of a glorious caitya for the pacification of sins;
he should worship it with pure devotion and honor it with the five types of offerings. ||11||
For one who takes refuge in the Three Jewels and possesses the supreme morality and vows,
there is indeed purity in this world and in the next.
Having intentionally violated a vow, he shall perform the vow for one year.
One should perform the vow for half a year in the case of one who was bound [to the act] unintentionally.
When half [of the required number] is completed, he should perform the fire-oblation and cause it to be given to the preceptor.
An unmeasured bracelet, clothing, a sacrificial fee, and food as well. ||14||
Then the virtuous monk, at the appropriate time, [should act] there for the sake of pacifying unwholesome states.
One should commence the worship of the ritual jar (kalaśa) and other items.
Immediately thereafter, one should bathe [the image] with the mantra of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
One should cause the purifying five products of the cow (pañcagavya) to be offered.
And in that regard, if even those who possess virtues and those who are virtuous have died as kinsmen... ||1||
In that regard, for the killing of a monk, the rule for expiation lasts for ten years;
one becomes purified by the gift of wealth after nine years and two months. ||1||
The "ten-month destroyer of monks" (daśamāsabhikṣughna) refers to this [period] beginning with the Poṣadha; beyond this, all the regulations are as previously stated. ||2||
And in that case, for one whose complexion has become like that of a broken Śiva-linga, there is a penance lasting up to eight years for the killing of a Kṣapaṇaka. ||3||

One is purified from [the sin of killing] a cat by giving wealth and other offerings for seven years plus eight months; one who kills a broken-colored Śiva-liṅga or a Jain mendicant (kṣapaṇaka) must perform [the same penance].
The vow of the *poṣadha*, and so forth.
From this point forward, all the ritual procedures are as previously described. ||2||
Thus, the wise man should understand that even in the case of killing, one must determine the respective portions for lesser or greater expiation.
And in that regard:
For the killing of a Brahmin, the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) lasts for eight years.
(22) By giving wealth and other offerings for more than seven years and four months, one becomes purified.
One who violates the vow of killing a Brahmin for eight months shall perform penance.
The observance of the poṣadha and other such vows, and so forth.
From this point onward, all the ritual procedures are as previously described.
And in that case, there is a rule for penance lasting up to six years for the killing of a Kṣatriya.
One is purified by the giving of wealth for five and a half years.
But for the killing of a Kṣatriya, one should perform this for six months.
The vow of the poṣadha and so forth, and so on.
Therefore, the entire ritual procedure is as previously described. ||1||
And in that case, the rule for expiation for the killing of a Vaiśya lasts for a period of four years.
The giving of wealth purifies [the transgression] for three years and eight months.
But a Vaiśya who kills [a cow] shall perform [this penance] for four months.
The vow of the *poṣadha* and so forth, and so on.
From this point forward, all the ritual procedures are as previously described. ||1||
And in that case, the rule for penance for killing a Śūdra lasts for a period of two years.
One year and ten months [of impurity] is purified by the giving of wealth and other such acts.
But for killing a Śūdra, one should perform penance for two months.
The observance of the *poṣadha* and other such vows, and so forth.
From this point onward, everything is of every kind, as previously stated. ||1||
And in that case, the rule for expiation for killing one of low birth is one year.
One becomes purified by giving wealth and other gifts for eleven months.
For thirty-two days, however, one should perform the rite for the destruction of those born of low families.
The vow beginning with "the consumption of herbs," and so forth.
From this point forward, all the ritual procedures are as previously described. (23) And therein:
Regarding the penances for killing a person of low caste, the specific application must be determined by considering the caste, capacity, and qualities [of the offender].
In that regard:
Now, the expiation for the killing of a woman is being stated.
Thus, the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇī woman is like the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa man.
Thus, the killing of a *kṣatriṇī* (a woman of the warrior caste) must be treated according to the expiation prescribed for the killing of a *kṣatriya*.
Thus, the killing of a Vaiśya woman must be performed according to the same expiation as the killing of a Vaiśya man.
Thus, the expiation for killing a Śūdra woman should be performed in the same manner as the expiation for killing a Śūdra man.
Thus, for the killing of a woman of low birth, the penance prescribed for those of low birth must be performed.
One may kill the wife of a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, even if she has been honored with salutations.
A woman shall likewise perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin for three years.
A killer of a child and one who is ungrateful [are excluded], even if they have been purified according to the Dharma.
Fire, one who has sought refuge, and a killer of a woman—these should not dwell with one for even a single night. ||2||
Thus, having killed his mother for ten months and that evil-doing friend, he was heartless.
Wandering as one observing the vow for killing a Brahmin, you shall roam the mortal world, bearing the head of Viśva on your shoulder.
And having killed a pregnant woman, one should observe the vow of celibacy.
Or twice as much again for the killing of a woman; this leads to hell. ||4||
And perform your own duty with freedom from greed, leading toward me as its goal and its downward path.
The ritual procedure for which... ||5||
When the body is afflicted by extreme illness, or when there is fear of kings, thieves, and the like;
And the ritual service to the Guru, the Devas, and the Fire, performed daily, destroys the faults of ignorance.
For both the householder and the student, the penance shall be twofold;
indeed, those two alone are prescribed in the rules according to the distinction between intentional and unintentional [acts]. (7)
But for one who acts unintentionally through ignorance, one should prescribe double the purification.
The expiation for abandoning [a child] should be known as double that for [abandoning] one who is capable of understanding.
(24) He whose years are eighty is considered an old man; however, sixteen years is the age of a child.
Or three persons afflicted by disease are worthy of the argha for atonement. ||9||
And even there, perceiving distress, he looked out toward the gateway.
It is extremely difficult to perform oneself; therefore, it is inexhaustible and twice as great [when performed for others]. ||10||
And [he considers] the place and time, as well as the power, caste, devotion, action, and sequence.
It should be given only after careful deliberation; from now on, there shall be no permission for fasting. ||11||
For one capable of performing expiation, [the duty is fulfilled] by means of the father, brother, or others, like horses.
That [debt] should be divided and paid; however, by other people, it should be paid doubled. ||12||
Now,
the distinction between what may and may not be approached for sexual intercourse, what may and may not be eaten, and what may or may not be touched is being explained.
In the case of the weak, as well as children and the elderly, one must act for their benefit;
otherwise, a fault would arise, and there would be no favor shown to them. ||2||
Whether out of affection, or through delusion, or from fear, or even out of ignorance—whosoever bestows favor, merit accrues to them. (3)
One who is established in the Dharma should diligently determine the penance by clearly taking into account the place, time, age, strength, and the nature of the sin. 4.
If, when the potter's wheel has been set in motion, his hair were to fall into the vessel,
he should observe the vow of conduct (śīlavrata) for three revolutions until it has been purified.
Having gone to women of the lowest castes, having eaten, drunk, or accepted gifts from them, one who falls from his vow and character is purified by the Tripravartana rite. ||2||
Having reached this state, the wives of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had sexual union with a Śūdra should likewise observe virtuous conduct and religious vows.
Those who have not yet given birth are purified at that time by means of penance.

The mother, the mother’s sister, the mother-in-law, the maternal uncle’s wife, the father’s sister, the wife of a paternal uncle, the wife of a friend, the wife of a pupil, and likewise the female friend of one’s own sister; ||4||

A daughter, the wife of a teacher, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge, those granted by a king, and those protected by a nurse—let there be no such [sexual union] with virtuous women. (25)
Having gone to another woman, he is called a violator of the guru's bed.
In that case, the student should perform the cutting; no other person is prescribed for this task.
Or else, he who has violated the teacher's bed shall practice celibacy.
For a man who is a killer of those born in the inverse order of castes or an adulterer, the manifestation of the vow [of the deity] before him is certain. 9.

The property of the gods, the property of the deity, the substance for the offering, the act of presenting the offering, the offering itself, and the substance of the moon—these are remembered as the six kinds of *nirmālya*. (10)
The property of one's own village and so forth is not "devadravya" (property belonging to a deity), such as cloth and other items.
An offering was prepared for him, consisting of the remnants of what had been offered to the deity.
That lunar substance, having been offered, is cast out as *nirmālya*.
Even the remains of the sacrificial cake (piṇḍikā) situated there, or the floral offerings (nirmālya), should not be discarded even by those who have been excluded from the deity's service.
A gift given to a wicked person does not become a vessel for that [merit] when it reaches him. ||12||
From taking [the substance] for its fragrance and so forth, there is smearing of the body, loss of accomplishment, and a wolf;
just as a man becomes a caṇḍāla through burning, such is the result in his prowess.
By touching it with women, it undoubtedly becomes like the remains of an offering (nirmālya). ||13||
One should not offer these to one's gurus, nor to sacred images, nor during scriptural expositions:
leaves, flowers, fruits, water, food, drink, clothing, or medicine.
But one should eat what has been prepared for food, provided it is not an offering.
Having fasted for a day and night, bathed, and being fully devoted to his vow, he becomes pure and stainless by drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) once. ||16||
One should avoid performing worship, giving gifts, or eating at night,
except during a lunar eclipse or when there is a desire for spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). ||17||

Bathing on occasions such as eclipses, weddings, the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), journeys, and times of distress is to be known as occasional (naimittika); it is prescribed even at night.
Water should be discarded during the middle two watches of the night;
one should not perform bathing there, nor the ritual of sipping water (ācamana). (26) 19.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should not eat; rather, having bathed when they are liberated [from the eclipse], one should give gifts.
If they have not been liberated, one should bathe at their setting and then eat on the following day.
Having bathed, or even having entered the water, or having touched it, or having taken hold of it, and having praised it by saying "Svasti," one is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Even when a house is burning or when human members of one's family have died, there is no taking of life among living beings therein; it is merely the burning of a house.
During divine processions, weddings, sacrificial rites,
and all festive occasions, it is not a fault whether one has been asked or not.

If one should touch something impure, that person alone becomes defiled; having touched it, others are not defiled by those [impurities], for this is the rule regarding the removal of taint from all castes.
Having touched a Divākīrti, a corpse, a person who has just given birth, or anything else belonging to her, one becomes pure by bathing. ||25||
During journeys, at the giving of gifts, during marriages, and in the context of sacrifices,
one should avoid food that has been touched by crows or mendicants.

The hand of an artisan is always pure; food placed on the hand of one who has paid his debt or extended for sale is pure; and food brought by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the established rule. (26)
The sons of one's father’s sister, the son of one's mother’s sister,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbandhu). ||27||
The mother's brother, the sister, and the sons; the son of the maternal uncle and the paternal aunt;
and the mother's mother's sons—these are to be known as the maternal relatives (mātṛbandhu). ||28||

And wherever such a relationship is possible, it is precisely there that [the lineage] extends to the seventh degree from those related on the father's side and from those related on the mother's side.
And marriage is to be observed [in this manner]. ||30||
And where this is so, it is not possible if there is no future manifestation.
In this matter, the paternal kin are to be regarded as the maternal kin, and the maternal relatives are to be regarded as the paternal relatives;
from these, seven generations on either side are to be seen as belonging to one's own lineage.
Thus [ends the section].
||31|| (27) One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one afflicted by disease;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive body hair, nor one whose hair is matted or reddish-brown. ||32||
She should not have the name of a die, a tree, or a river; nor should she bear the name of a mountain.
She should not be named after a bird, a snake, or a flower, nor should she have a terrifying nose. (33)
He should not marry a woman who has missing limbs, nor one who is a wanderer by name, nor one with sparse teeth or hair, but rather one with soft limbs. 34.
Possessing gold and silver, as well as noble birth, beauty, youth, and learning, he gave his son to you in accordance with dharma, yet he himself was one who gave little in charity. (35)
Having collected eight, seven, or five alms, and having prepared them without fail, O best of the twice-born, he should then eat with self-restraint. (36)
There is no begging for food from others, nor is there the acceptance of alms;
day after day, one partakes of the drinking of Soma from both the Avadhūta and the Pūta.
Even if an outcaste or one fallen from his caste remains hidden there,
once he has been properly identified after some time, one should then carry out purification.
Regarding what was stated there concerning cooked food, it is distinct from what has been previously described;
by fasting for one day for each [offense], one should not consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). ||39||
They know that for all those of other castes, one should perform ritual sipping (ācamana) after touching them;
however, when one eats after having touched such a person, a full bath is prescribed for him.
Oil that has become rancid, as well as unctuous substances derived from fruits,
are considered pure even when they have been transferred into vessels belonging to Mlecchas. ||41||
The handling of leather and meat, as well as purification and kindling,
the purification of the *puṇāśruka* and *śrukā*, and the conduct of one who has risen [from impurity] are now described.
During marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, as well as during the intervening periods of death or birth impurity,
material that was previously intended for a purpose is not defiled when it is being given away.
If one is unable due to circumstances such as fear or festivities, one may act according to one's convenience;
however, at the time of giving, one should reflect upon the fact that the excellence of ethical discipline (*śīla*) has been described as being dependent [on generosity].
(44) Thinking thus, one should then generate [the intention] to practice it.
That very thing must be accomplished here with an inner self absorbed in that. ||45||
For if this is done, all will be well; otherwise, there will be fear for us. Even one who is hairless shall attain growth as he proceeds. (46)
Thus ends the section on penance regarding those who may or may not be approached for intercourse, and those things that may or may not be eaten.

Just as it was heard and just as it was seen by the unimpeded gurus, so too is the transgression of that [teaching] through its violation in contradiction with one's own established tenets and so forth. (13)
An excellent son, even when struck by his mother, father, or brother,
is not tainted by sin if he dies as a result of that beating.
If that servant, acting for the benefit [of his master] or being oppressed by the wealthy master, strikes him and he dies as a result, he is not tainted by the sin. ||15||
His father, the elder monk, being urged on, quickly departed;
today, as he has died, [the offense] is immediate.
It is joined. ||16||
If a sick person, having been struck by a malignant spirit, exerts pressure on his own throat, and the attendant monk dies, that monk incurs no fault. //17//
"One who excessively exceeds the knowledge of others incurs fault";
thus it was clearly stated in the Vinaya that there is no fault for those with corrupt minds. ||18||
In the section on the rules for expiation, purification, and conduct, this is the chapter on the arising of expiation.
In the section on the rules for expiation, purification, and conduct, this is the chapter on the arising of expiation.
Now, in establishing the rules regarding the expiation for killing a cow,
the scope of the rule for the expiation for killing a Vaiśya is established by way of analogy with the expiation for cow-slaughter.
The expiation for the killing of a cow is not the same as the expiation for the killing of a Vaiśya. ||2||
He should give a bull or a cow together with a complete atonement;
whoever kills my ox, he shall give me a bull.
One who has killed a cow should observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) continuously for one month while possessing cattle;
by giving cows, gold, and other such gifts, he is released from the sin of killing a cow.
(29) Even in the case of consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the killer of a cow is purified by [the recitation of] the *Māṣamaithuna* hymn.
One who has lived for a year among cattle in a cow-pen is purified by the gift of a cow. ||4||
When they destroy [beings] somewhere by means of their hideous forms, those who are agitated, terrified, or even dead shall incur the fault. ||5||
He was struck with a wooden stick by the cowherd for the purpose of driving the cow;
consequently, he incurred the sin of cow-slaughter at the end of his life.
One should observe the vow at the time of the essence of the cow (godhna-sāra), providing gold, clothing, and food;
by shedding one's nails and hair, one is liberated within a fortnight.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and a cow;
thus one becomes free from sin, even in the case of many acts of pleasing [others], or in captivity or imprisonment.
If one person, or even many,
should at any time commit a portion of the sin of killing, they shall each perform a quarter of that penance individually.

Through excessive exertion, through being struck down, through the binding of a yoke-strap, through crossing a river with a stream of caustic salt, and likewise through being bitten and through falling down. ||10||
One quarter [of the penance] applies when obstructing [the flow], two quarters when binding [it], and three-quarters when causing the loss of all the flavors of the food. (11)
In the case of medical treatment involving restraint, or in an effort to release a concealed fetus,
if death should occur despite the effort being made, no expiation is required.
If misfortune should occur while giving medicine, oil, or food to cows and Brahmins, he is not tainted by that sin. (13)
If one undergoes burning, cutting, or the breaking of the head with great effort for the sake of the welfare of men or cattle, no penance is prescribed. (14)
If the fetus should perish due to the striking down of cows, one *kṛcchra* penance shall be performed for each [cow], as previously prescribed and likewise thereafter. (15)
When only one foot has arisen, two feet are established upon the body;
when the feet do not move toward the vow, he is not conscious of having struck the body.
Having pulled out all the hair, this [act] is to be cut with two fingers.
In the same way, for women, shaving the head is prescribed as the rite of tonsure. ||17||
In the case of cows that have perished in the dwellings of temple-servants, in wells, or in sacred shrines— there is no expiation required for these. (18)
Those wicked ones who strike down inferiors with a stone, in the anus, or even with a weapon, must perform the Kṛcchra penance for purification. (19)
This very [act] was done by me for the sake of concealing [the truth] from my wife, due to the bond of worldly flow;
as for those [acts] committed during marriages, no expiation is prescribed. (20)
Whether he is unconscious, purified, or even struck by an arrow,
when the animal follows the path of the *ruṃchitā* [sacrificial cord] for fifteen or seventeen steps, [the sacrifice is successful].
If one should take up the water from the house during bathing, one should drink it oneself;
when all diseases have been destroyed by this, no expiation is required. ||22||
The conclusion of the second section on expiation for cow-slaughter within the rules for purification through penance and conduct.
When a death that has reached completion occurs, no impurity (āśauca) should be observed there among all castes, even for a sapinda relative. ||48||
In the event of a house fire, or when a cow, a child, or a human being has died, what is the expiation there, by what means is it performed, and how is the ground purified? (49)
"Remain here until friendship with the entire [community] is established; and when it has taken root among the virtuous, then the ground becomes pure. (50)
Carrying a trident in her hand or lying on the ground at night in an earthen vessel, she remains in her menstrual state;
on the fourth day, having bathed, she shall attain purity.

If a maiden in her father’s house has her menses after [the marriage] but is not consecrated by the *sabhya* rite, she incurs the sin of foeticide for her father; such a maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*. (52)

He who, with a mind deluded by greed, marries such a girl—he is a transgressor of the bounds of propriety; know him to be the husband of a *vṛṣalī*. (52) Both the mother and the father, as well as the elder brother who gave her away, [are likewise at fault].
All those who, upon seeing girls who have reached their menses, [fail to act properly], go to hell. ||53||
Therefore, one should marry off a maiden before she reaches puberty.
The marriage of an eight-year-old girl is commended by the wise. ||54||
As long as she does not recognize shame, and as long as she plays with her kinsmen.
One should marry off the daughter at that time, as proclaimed by the sages. ||55||

For the sake of destroying the impurity of sin, even a maiden may, by means of the prescribed rite, become one who has undergone sacrifice for her husband; yet she shall not be liberated from her lord without him.
If a wife, having abandoned her husband and son through unjust conduct,
dies there, then for her, purification is achieved after three nights of ritual voiding.
To one who is eminent, well-born, suitable, and excellent.
To him who has arrived, the father should give his daughter according to the prescribed rite.
If the husband of a maiden for whom the nuptial fee has been paid should die,
she should be given to his brother, provided that the maiden consents.
"At that time, this substance must be handed over to her. ||61||

The acceptance of wives from among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras constitutes the excellence of one's own caste; such a wife is the means for the performance of the highest rites, just as gold is for the performance of sacrificial acts.
If a woman dies while still belonging to her paternal lineage (sagotra), she shall be married at the seventh step;
her funeral rites, such as the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), must be performed using the husband’s lineage.

During vows, festivals, and weddings, as well as at the moment of death or birth-impurity, one should perform all rites immediately; however, for other acts, it should be done after one day, provided they have not been previously heard [of].
Let those who desire her go; let the groom of this maiden of equal caste take her away, having adorned her according to the rule—he alone shall marry her. (65)
If one eats from a single vessel, or if there is contact with the mouth at the door of the house, there shall be *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) for them both upon birth and upon death. 66.
As long as that lineage-sproout exists through the fourth generation, so long does it obtain inheritance;
but by the fifth, the offspring [is severed]... (67)
In the fourth [case], purification occurs after ten nights; in the fifth, after fifteen days;
in the sixth, after four days; but in the seventh, after one day and night.
In the case of a Maitreya, an Ātreya, a royal prince, a daughter’s son, a sister’s son, a Sāluka,
or one equal to him, one becomes pure after three nights. ||69||

One who has performed the Daśarātra, the Atirātra, and the Trirātra sacrifices is considered pure; likewise, one who has experienced the birth-impurity (sūtaka) previously and again experiences it for the family (kula-sūtaka). 70.
For three nights, the wife of an Atri shall subsist on Śāli rice;
after that year has passed, she becomes pure by bathing immediately.
For those children who die at birth or immediately upon emerging from the womb when ignorance has arisen, there is no cremation with fire, nor impurity, nor water-libations. (72)
If a miscarriage occurs or if a woman dies while pregnant,
the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had been in the womb.
If the rite of initiation (*vrata-saṃskāra*) has been neglected for ten years, you shall observe impurity (*aśauca*) for that many days; this is declared by Dadhīci and Dakṣa. (74)
As long as a woman is not cut [by the rite], she does not incur the state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*);
once she has been cut, thereafter the *sūtaka* is prescribed. ||75–76||
Thus ends the fourth chapter on purification within the rules for penance, purity, and conduct.
Now the section on purity and impurity begins:
One who possesses knowledge, who constantly worships the gods and the sacred fire, is purified after one day from the birth or death of a deceased person when it concerns a Vajrācārya. (1)
A virtuous and ethical monk who is constantly devoted to the Dharma is purified immediately upon bathing, even after the birth or death of a deceased person. ||2||
For every renunciant, even one accompanied by ten disciples,
if he remains attached to the duties of a householder, there shall be an ill omen for seven days. (33)
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month. (4)
Impurity due to birth is prescribed for ten days among sapinda relatives; however, if the bones are collected before that time, the impurity lasts for one day.
On the fourth day, for one who has died within the Kārṣṇājini lineage, the collection [of bones] is to be performed;
after that collection, however, no [further rite] is prescribed for the limb.
Then, by means of rising from study together with the practice of yoga, one becomes pure;
by the practice of mere study, one becomes pure in four days. ||7||
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and is devoted to the Vedas is purified in one day;
for those who lack these, and for others who are even lower, purification takes four days and four nights respectively.

For those Brahmins who merely bear the name [of their caste] but have not witnessed [their own] birth-rites and are devoid of immediate worship [of the deity], the period of impurity (sutaka) shall last for ten days. ||9||
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Brāhmaṇas—these are his four classes [of attendants].
The collection of the bones should be observed on the fourth day as well. ||4||
Those Śūdras who are purified by the scriptures and are constantly devoted to their duty are cleansed within half a month; indeed, they are not equal to ordinary Śūdras.
A farmer who is not a Śūdra is likewise purified in twelve days;
these twelve days consist of the ritual of fire-worship, recitation of hymns, and the performance of rites of omission.
Just as this impurity on account of a corpse is prescribed for the sapinda relatives, so too should it be observed for the mother by one who desires precise purity. (10)

For all [relatives], there is impurity (āśauca) for ten days; however, regarding the birth-impurity (sūtaka) of the parents, it belongs to the mother alone. The father, having performed ritual sipping (upaspṛśya), becomes pure.
In the case of a son born [to him], the father’s bath with his clothes is prescribed;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, while for the preceptor it is gradual, like that of the father.
And when a child is staying in another country and his funeral cake has been separately and properly established, he becomes purified immediately by bathing in all the waters. (34) 13.

One should observe impurity for one's own sister, for a sister of one's mother, for a maternal uncle, for a maternal uncle's wife, and for a father-in-law; during this period, one should spend the night in a secluded place.
Having touched a divākīrti, one who has applied unguents, an outcaste, or likewise earth, as well as having touched the touch of a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing. ||15||

For a deceased woman who was menstruating, the rites such as prostrations and so forth should be performed after she has been bathed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder; this should be made known in all religious duties.
Even one who belongs to another lineage, if he offers the funeral fire for a deceased person,
he must provide water, fire, and the rice-ball offerings (piṇḍas) for ten days, bathing immediately thereafter.
Just as these statements are common to all castes, so too should those that set forth specific [distinctions] be regarded as such;
for there is no evidence for specific [distinctions]. ||18||
If one desires to die again within that intermediate period of ten days, one must remain pure with devotion for as long as it takes to emerge from hell. 19.
Even if the mother, who is the primary knower, is impure, she may be purified by the remaining [purificatory rites] of the father; however, one should perform the Yakṣiṇī rite for the mother.
At every death, there is no son, nor indeed is there a dead one.
Whichever of the two occurs first, by that period of impurity one becomes pure. ||21||
One becomes pure by means of a dead body, but a corpse does not become pure by means of a birth-impurity.
A short [syllable] should not follow a pure short [syllable], nor should a long [syllable] follow a short [syllable]. ||22||
In the case of birth-impurity or death-impurity, there may likewise be birth-impurity within death-impurity;
the impure is purified by the corpse, but the corpse is not purified by purification. ||23||
But if one hears that [a relative] who has gone abroad and resides in a foreign land has died at a distance of ten *yojanas*,
that period of impurity shall last for ten nights, and one remains pure only after that time.

Having heard of the death of a distant relative and the birth of a son, one becomes pure by bathing in water at night; so says Mādhava. (25) But upon the death of a great guru, having placed [the body] in wet cloth...
Regarding those who have passed away, one should perform the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules.
Furthermore, after the death of a paternal uncle or an aunt, a person remains impure for three nights, even if a year has elapsed since the mother’s death. (27)
If the relatives of a Brahmin are Kṣetriṇīs or Śūdra heirs, the purification for that Brahmin is held to occur after ten days, even during their period of impurity. 28.
If a Kṣatriya kills a Vaiśya, or if he kills relatives born of a lower caste, they must perform their own period of impurity for the sake of purification; of this there is no doubt. (29)

One should observe purity toward all those of lower status as one would toward a mother; however, regarding one's own kin, one should perform the respective purification according to the rules prescribed for that specific caste.
If many sons born of one [father] have separate ears and noses, their impurity is that of the father; however, after the father's death, it is separate for each.
When there is a single husband for women of the various castes in their respective order,
if he should give birth to children on the same day, the period of impurity (sutaka) shall last ten days, six days, three days, and one day respectively.
When a son has died, the purification for the female slaves and wives shall follow the order of their seniority;
when the master has died, the purification is that of a son.
Relatives are purified in five days from those [women] who have previously had another husband or who are forbidden;
for those other than these, purification is prescribed in five days. (34)
Having been instructed, one should prepare a sweetmeat (modaka) to be presented upon the arrival [of the guest];
on the seventh day, one should prepare water from the earth, and for three nights one remains impure.
The king should not [punish] those who drink liquor, nor those devoted to women, nor those of the kṣatriya caste,
if those brāhmaṇas who occupy the station of Indra have been remembered by him.
The water libation shall cease for those born of mixed castes, for those who remain in the state of wandering mendicants, and for those who have renounced their own lives. (36)

And for those who have taken refuge in heretics, as well as for kings who kill [their subjects] or those who act according to their own whims—even for gods—there is no water-libation or food-offering for those who commit suicide. (38) Indeed, lightning, a king, a Brahmin, a horned animal, and one who kills a cow are not considered perpetrators of sin. (36)
A eunuch, one who causes distress, and one who eats food [belonging to others] are not fit for the water-vow (udaka-vrata), just like those who have taken other vows. ||39||
If someone dies through [an act of] grace by means of fire, water, or the like, impurity must be observed for him, and the water-libation rites must be performed. (40)
From a Cāṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent... even from a Brāhmaṇa;
and from [evil] sights and from beasts that bring about death through their harmful deeds. (41)

One should cause the recitation of the Śānti for those who have been struck down by all [calamities], by female jackals, by evil glances, or by kings, as well as for those who have abandoned their own lives. 42.
Whatever water or food offerings are presented to the gurus, none of it remains; it dissolves into the intermediate space. ||43||
But if he passes away before the ten nights have elapsed, both the mother and the father—a Brahmin or a non-Brahmin—become pure by means of a ritual bath. (44)

From a slave to a slave, and so forth for all [castes], whatever may be the caste of one's master, the purification for that caste shall apply; likewise, the period of impurity following death or birth (sūtaka) is the same as that of the master. 45.
In times of famine, when kingdoms are in turmoil, and especially during periods of great distress,
as well as in the case of death by calamity, immediate purification is ordained.

If a living being were to die immediately after being born, or if one who was dead were to be born again, then the rule of dharma would be that impurity (sūtaka) must be observed in those cases. ||47||
If a child dies within ten days, his kinsmen shall not observe impurity;
he is pure, for he is purified by that very purity.
Now, beginning with the rules for the *śrāddha*: on the day [of death], the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) and the water-rites must be performed by the son for his father;
in the absence of a son, it shall be done by the wife; and in the absence of a wife, by a uterine brother. (1)
For year after year, those rites for one's mother and father must indeed be performed; at the Śrāddha, one should feed a non-devotee and offer a single rice-ball (piṇḍa). (2) (37)
The husband should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for his wife, and likewise the wife for her husband;
the same applies to sisters and others, and in their absence, one who observes the vow of chastity [should do so].
For those who have died without sons—whether they be women or even men—the Koddista and Parvana rites must indeed be performed for them as well. (4)

The daily rite (nitya), the occasional rite (naimittika), the rite for prosperity (vṛddhi-śrāddha), and furthermore the ancestral rite on specific lunar days (pārvaṇa)—these are known by the wise as the five types of śrāddha. ||5||
The *palyūrvāhna* [śrāddha] is for the ancestors at midday, while the *paitṛka* is at afternoon; the *diṣṭa* is performed alone at midday, and that caused by prosperity (*vṛddhi*) is in the morning.
One should feed a well-nourished preceptor who is knowledgeable in the ritual procedures,
but one should not feed a foolish person who is fasting, or rather, one should feed him comfortably.
If an obstacle arises to the *śrāddha* for one who has died on a day of prescribed merit (*vidhitejina*),
it should be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) or, especially, on a pure day.
Upon the death of a great preceptor (mahāguru), one should not perform ritual bathing, great acts of charity, Vedic study, or the offering of libations for one full year.
Kalaśas, sesame seeds, elephants, a female slave, land, a chariot, a house, a maiden, and a tawny cow—these are the ten great gifts (mahādānas). 10.
The intercalary month (adhimāsa) should not be used for rites such as the annual Śrāddha;
however, rites such as the birth-anniversary ceremony (varṣavṛddhi) and royal consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed using the intercalary month.
Even those [acts] that are auspicious during the [forbidden] months should be performed by high-souled men;
however, one who desires his own welfare should not perform what is inauspicious. 12.
Betel, drinking milk, wearing flowers, anointing the body with unguents, cleaning the teeth, and collyrium are not impaired by fasting. (13)
The performance of a separate Śrāddha for the mother has not been proclaimed by the Teacher;
in that vessel containing the rice-balls and water for the ancestors, the virtuous wife is the one who receives the first portion. 14.
May those who are born in low families, those who are childless, and those who are kinless;
those who are deformed, those who have died in the womb, and those known or unknown in my family—may they be satisfied by what is given upon the earth and attain the supreme goal. (15) (38)

For the purification of the path devoid of ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), one should practice the *svadhā*-limb [of the ritual], beginning with the *saṃskāra* of the crow and so forth, as well as the baths and so forth— even at an improper time for bathing— while reciting, "I offer this *piṇḍa*."
When milk is offered for the sake of the deceased by his own kinsmen to the preceptor, it should be understood as being given to him; that milk-offering belongs to the one who has departed to heaven.
It should be given by his relatives seven days prior;
by that gift, he shall be taken up to Sukhāvatī. ||18||
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water boiled with kuśa grass—this is designated as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which is purifying and cleanses the body. 19.
The cow’s urine should come from a blue cow, the cow dung from a black one;
the milk from a copper-colored cow, and the curd from a white, fragrant cow.
The ghee of a tawny cow (kapilā) should be taken, for it destroys great sins; especially so in the absence of [ghee] from all other castes. ||20||
Therefore, one should employ the materials from a tawny cow as they are obtained:
one should give the entire amount of cow urine, half a thumb’s measure of cow dung,
seven palas of milk, and five palas of curd.
One should offer a single pala of mercury, along with water for sipping (ācamana) and water from a sacred site (tīrtha),
having placed it upon a copper plate according to all the prescribed rites.
Elsewhere also it is stated that on the day [of the rite], one *pala* each of cow’s ghee, cow dung,
and cow urine is prescribed; one should give seven *palas* of milk and five *palas* of curd.
O Maitreya, one should fashion five palas of gold into the form of the Sun,
according to the auspicious ritual procedure.
One should give [the thread] to a worthy person according to the teacher's instruction, along with water from a sacred site (tīrtha),
for the destruction of all sins, for the purpose of worship, and for purification.
O Lord of Great Compassion,
grant me the five products of the cow for the sake of purifying body, speech, and mind, and for the cleansing of the miserable realms.
And: (39) O Great Compassionate One, Protector,
grant me the five products of the cow.
Born from all the Victors without exception, the purifier of all realms—
O Lord of Great Compassion,
grant me the five sense objects. (22)
One pala of cow urine, half an aṅguṣṭha of cow dung,
seven palas of milk should be given, and three palas of curd are prescribed.
One should give one pala of āpāmaarga and one pala of kuśa-water;
having prepared the ghee separately, one should then mix it with the other ingredients.
One should present the five products of the cow through the hand of the senior member of the assembly;
by this, the body and mind are purified, and then food may be given for consumption.
One should worship that according to one's ability, especially with robes and other requisites;
it is to be worshipped with the fivefold offering, as well as through devotion of body, speech, and material gifts. ||25||
By this indeed.
Oṃ hruṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ aḥ.
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having fasted for a day and night and bathed, one should drink that [mixture] facing east;
having drunk the auspicious *pañcagavya* once, it should be consecrated with the sacred mantras.
Freed from all evil, the human being becomes pure.
Thus ends the section on Śrāddha within the rules for purification and conduct in the ordinance of expiation.
